messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi was thirty-seven years old, a clinical psychologist living in a Midwestern suburb with his wife, Priya. Eighteen months earlier, he had been two blocks from a downtown holiday market when a lone attacker opened fire with a rifle. The shots came in a sudden, tearing sequence—pop-pop-pop—just as he was stepping out of his office building. He had no time to think, only to drop to the ground behind a concrete planter, his heart slamming against his ribs while bodies around him scrambled and fell. For what felt like an eternity, he lay there with his hands pressed over his ears, utterly certain that the next sound would be the one that ended him. He did not see the attacker, but he felt the absolute dissolution of any control he had ever imagined having over his own safety. When the shooting stopped and police swarmed the area, he walked back to his car on legs that would not stop trembling, and he drove home in silence.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi told himself he was fine. He had treated trauma survivors for years; he knew the signs intellectually. But his own experience refused to stay on the page. At night, he woke in the dark with a jolt, his hands already reaching for something, his breath shallow, convinced that someone was inside the house. He could not fall back asleep unless he had a drink—at first one, then two, then three. Alcohol became the only thing that quieted the hypervigilance, the constant scanning for danger that had taken up residence behind his ribs. He started to avoid anything that felt even remotely stressful. At work, he stopped taking new clients who had histories of violence or sudden loss. He steered every intake toward what he called “low-acuity” cases, knowing full well that he was shrinking his practice, his professional identity, by the week. His colleagues noticed, and he made excuses—burnout, a need to simplify his caseload. What he could not tell them was that the sight of a client in tears now sent him into a cold sweat, because it reminded him of that afternoon when he had been equally powerless, and powerlessness now felt like the only truth that mattered.

His marriage began to fray. Priya would reach for him at night and find him rigid, staring at the ceiling. She would ask what was wrong, and he would say nothing, because how could he explain that he had come to believe the world was a place where catastrophe could arrive without warning, that he could not stop it, and that the person lying next to her, the psychologist who used to offer calm and reason, had been replaced by someone he barely recognised? He had started drifting off into elaborate daydreams during the afternoon, constructing whole alternate lives in his head—a quiet cottage by the sea where no one could find him, where no sounds ever startled. It was the only time he felt any relief, but it also meant that Priya had to repeat things to him three times before he heard her. Once, she asked if he even wanted to be with her anymore. He had no answer that made sense.

What finally brought Ravi to this office—his own therapist’s office, something he had put off for nearly a year—was a single moment two weeks ago. He was walking to his car after an evening session when a teenager in the parking lot accidentally slammed a car door. The sound tore through him like the first shot. He dropped his briefcase, his knees buckled, and for ten seconds he stood frozen in the dark, gasping, unsure where he was. A security guard came over and asked if he was all right. Ravi said yes, but he was not. He got in his car and drove home and poured himself a drink with shaking hands, and that night he told Priya he needed help. He is sitting here now, across from a stranger, terrified that talking about it will make it worse, and equally terrified that not talking about it will cost him everything he still has left.
